one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban welcomes Pope Leo XIV -- the first American-born, Augustinian-educated, Peruvian missionary who chose seminary over a Harvard law scholarship -- as the 'pope of the peripheries' who personifies Vatican II's reforms (continued by Saint Pope John Paul II and Pope Francis, and implemented in the Philippines via PCP II in 1991, in which the author participated as one of a few invited laypersons). At his first Mass in the Sistine Chapel, Pope Leo XIV stressed bridge-building faith, preferring mission over structures and dogmas, and reducing the Ten Commandments to the two great love commands -- echoing the final judgment scene in Matthew 25:31-46. The author reads the new pontiff's vision through Pope Francis's Singapore line that 'all religions are pathways to God,' and quotes Pope Leo XIV's motto 'In illo uno unum. In the One, we are one.' Cardinal Ambo David's pastoral invitation, with Cardinals Tagle and Advincula seconding, drew the Pope's 'If God allows it' reply; the author suggests President Marcos add a sovereign-to-sovereign invitation given the Pope also heads the Holy See. He teases his Trumpist friends that their hero is now 'only the second most important American in the world' and that 'MAGA now means Make America Godly Again,' but notes US Republican-leaning conservatism's contradictions -- including Trump's deportation of migrants without due process, recently stopped by even the conservative SCOTUS. He pivots to Dobbs v. Jackson (June 24, 2022) overturning Roe v. Wade, then to PH doctrine: Imbong v. Ochoa (April 4, 2014, per J. Mendoza, en banc, 11-1-3) categorically held life begins at fertilization, making the zygote a human being whose killing is a crime -- consistent with the Constitution's pro-life orientation. He predicts Pope Leo XIV and the CBCP will strengthen opposition to bills reimposing the death penalty and legislating absolute divorce, and discloses that as an incumbent justice he consistently believed the death penalty unconstitutional, carrying on the crusade backed by one or two justices until Congress and President Arroyo repealed the law.
